title: September 2021 Class College Final Supplementary Exam (Part 3 of 6)
unit: Comprehensive Nursing (Men's Health, Dermatology, Cardiovascular, Renal and Urology, Respiratory, Neurology, Emergency, Gerontology)

sets.title: Set 1: Original Exam Questions
sets.description: The original MCQs from the September 2021 class College Final Supplementary Exam paper (Kenya Registered Nursing, sat 30 May 2024, Multiple Choice Questions, Q41 to Q60).

questions.text: Features of Andropause include:

options.A: Decreased abdominal fat, decreased erectile quality
options.B: Decreased body hair, decreased volume of ejaculate
options.C: Increased sexual desire, increased bone mass density

questions.explanation: Decreased body hair, decreased volume of ejaculate (B) is correct because andropause (late-onset hypogonadism) is the age-related fall in testosterone in men, which causes decreased body hair, reduced volume of ejaculate, reduced muscle mass and strength, fatigue, low mood, poor concentration, reduced libido and reduced bone density. Decreased abdominal fat, decreased erectile quality (A) is incorrect because the erectile quality does fall, but abdominal fat increases (central obesity) with low testosterone. Increased sexual desire, increased bone mass density (C) is incorrect because libido and bone density both decrease (osteoporosis risk). Erectile dysfunction, increased nocturnal erections (D) is incorrect because erectile dysfunction occurs, but nocturnal erections decrease.

questions.text: A skin condition that presents with ‘cobblestone’, redness and tenderness of lower extremity is:
questions.explanation: Cellulitis (A) is correct because it is an acute bacterial infection (usually Streptococcus or Staphylococcus aureus) of the dermis and subcutaneous tissue, most often of the lower leg, which presents with a warm, red, swollen, tender area with poorly defined edges; the oedema can give the skin a cobblestone or peau d'orange appearance, and there may be fever and lymphangitis. Erysipelas (B) is incorrect because it involves the upper dermis and lymphatics, and it presents as a bright red, raised, sharply demarcated plaque, usually on the face or leg, without the cobblestone appearance. Impetigo (C) is incorrect because it is a superficial skin infection with honey-coloured crusted lesions, mostly in children. Viral warts (D) are incorrect because they are painless, rough, raised growths caused by human papillomavirus.

questions.text: Forms of distributive shock include:
questions.explanation: Septic, anaphylactic (A) is correct because distributive (vasodilatory) shock is caused by widespread vasodilation and increased capillary permeability, so the blood is maldistributed and the effective circulating volume is low even though the total volume is normal; the three forms are septic, anaphylactic and neurogenic shock. Cardiogenic, hypovolemic (B) is incorrect because cardiogenic shock is pump failure and hypovolaemic shock is a loss of circulating volume, and they are separate categories. Neurogenic, hypovolemic (C) is incorrect because neurogenic shock is distributive but hypovolaemic is not. Anaphylactic, cardiogenic (D) is incorrect because anaphylactic shock is distributive but cardiogenic is not. Obstructive shock (for example tension pneumothorax, cardiac tamponade and pulmonary embolism) is the fourth category.

questions.text: The angina due to coronary artery spasm is:
questions.explanation: Variant (B) is correct because variant (Prinzmetal) angina is caused by spasm of a coronary artery, usually at rest, often at night or in the early morning, with transient ST elevation on the ECG, and it responds to calcium channel blockers and nitrates. Silent angina (A) is incorrect because it is myocardial ischaemia without symptoms, common in diabetic patients. Stable angina (C) is incorrect because it is predictable chest pain on exertion or stress from fixed coronary atherosclerosis, relieved by rest or nitrates. Unstable angina (D) is incorrect because it is new, worsening or rest pain from a ruptured plaque with thrombus, and it is an acute coronary syndrome that needs urgent care.

questions.text: Central venous pressure monitoring is indicated for estimation of:
questions.explanation: Preload (B) is correct because the central venous pressure (CVP), measured with a catheter in the superior vena cava or right atrium (normal 2 to 8 mmHg, or 3 to 10 cm of water), reflects the pressure of blood returning to the right side of the heart, that is, the right ventricular filling pressure or preload, and it is used to assess fluid status and the response to fluid replacement. Afterload (A) is incorrect because it is the resistance against which the ventricle ejects, estimated by the systemic vascular resistance. Left atrium pressure (C) and left ventricular pressure (D) are incorrect because they are left-heart pressures, estimated with a pulmonary artery catheter (pulmonary artery wedge pressure) and not by the CVP.

questions.text: In an ECG strip, ventricular repolarization is represented by:
questions.explanation: T wave (C) is correct because the T wave represents repolarisation (recovery) of the ventricles, which follows the QRS complex. P wave (A) is incorrect because it represents atrial depolarisation. R wave (B) is incorrect because it is the first upward deflection of the QRS complex, which represents ventricular depolarisation (atrial repolarisation is hidden within the QRS). U wave (D) is incorrect because it is a small wave sometimes seen after the T wave, which is thought to be repolarisation of the Purkinje fibres and is prominent in hypokalaemia.

questions.text: The SA Node fires at a rate of:
questions.explanation: 60-100 b/min (C) is correct because the sinoatrial (SA) node is the natural pacemaker of the heart and has the fastest intrinsic firing rate, 60 to 100 impulses per minute, which sets the normal sinus rhythm. 10-20 b/min (A) is incorrect because it is not the rate of any normal pacemaker site. 30-50 b/min (B) is incorrect because the 40 to 60 b/min rate is the AV junction rate, and the 20 to 40 b/min rate is the ventricular (Purkinje fibre) escape rate, and they take over only if the SA node fails. Above 100 b/min (D) is incorrect because it is tachycardia.

questions.text: A complication of ureteral strictures is:
questions.explanation: Hydronephrosis (A) is correct because a ureteric stricture narrows the ureter and obstructs the flow of urine from the kidney, so urine backs up into the renal pelvis and calyces, causing dilatation (hydronephrosis), and if it is not relieved it leads to infection (pyelonephritis), stone formation and progressive loss of kidney function. Urine retention (B) is incorrect because it describes obstruction at the bladder outlet or urethra (for example benign prostatic hyperplasia or urethral stricture). Cystitis (C) is incorrect because it is a bladder infection, a lower tract problem, which is not the direct complication of a ureteric stricture. Cystolithiasis (D) is incorrect because it means bladder stones, which are mainly associated with bladder outlet obstruction and stasis.

questions.text: The most appropriate test for staging of prostate cancer is:
questions.explanation: Magnetic resonance imaging (A) is correct because MRI shows the extent of the tumour within and beyond the prostate capsule (extracapsular extension, seminal vesicle invasion) and lymph node involvement, so it is the best imaging for local staging (a bone scan is added for bone metastases). Digital rectal examination (B) is incorrect because it is a screening and clinical examination that can detect a hard, irregular nodule but is not accurate for staging. Prostate specific antigen (C) is incorrect because it is a blood test used for screening, for assessing the risk and for monitoring the response to treatment, and it does not give the anatomical stage. Intravenous urography (D) is incorrect because it shows the urinary tract (for example hydronephrosis from obstruction) but not the extent of the cancer. The diagnosis itself is confirmed by transrectal ultrasound-guided biopsy with Gleason grading.

questions.text: Acute asthma is relieved by administration of:
questions.explanation: Salbutamol (C) is correct because it is a short-acting beta-2 agonist (SABA), the first-line reliever for an acute asthma attack, which relaxes the bronchial smooth muscle within minutes and is given by metered dose inhaler with a spacer or by nebuliser. Formoterol (A) is incorrect because it is a long-acting beta-2 agonist (LABA) used for maintenance with an inhaled corticosteroid, and it is not used alone. Cromolyn (D) is incorrect because it is a mast cell stabiliser used for prevention and not for relief of an attack. Terbutaline (B) is incorrect only in the sense that it is the less commonly used reliever: it is also a short-acting beta-2 agonist, but salbutamol is the standard drug of choice taught in Kenya. Note: because terbutaline is also a valid reliever, check this item against the marking scheme.

questions.text: The following are frequent side effects of Ipratropium bromide:
questions.explanation: Dry mouth, blurred vision (A) is correct because ipratropium bromide is an inhaled anticholinergic (antimuscarinic) bronchodilator, and blocking acetylcholine produces the typical anticholinergic effects: dry mouth, blurred vision (especially if the drug gets into the eyes, which can precipitate glaucoma), urinary retention, constipation and tachycardia. Salivation and diarrhoea (B) are incorrect because they are cholinergic effects, the opposite of an anticholinergic. Bradycardia and headache (C) are incorrect because anticholinergics cause tachycardia, and not bradycardia. Nausea and gait loss (D) are incorrect because they are not characteristic of this drug.

questions.text: The respiratory disease characterized by destruction of pulmonary capillary network and alveoli is:
questions.explanation: Emphysema (D) is correct because it is a form of COPD in which the walls of the alveoli (and their capillary beds) are destroyed, so the air spaces enlarge permanently, the surface for gas exchange is lost and the lungs lose their elastic recoil, causing air trapping, a barrel chest, dyspnoea and pursed-lip breathing (the main cause is cigarette smoking). Asthma (A) is incorrect because it is reversible airway inflammation and bronchospasm. Bronchiectasis (B) is incorrect because it is permanent dilatation and damage of the bronchi, with chronic sputum production. Chronic bronchitis (C) is incorrect because it is inflammation of the bronchi with excess mucus and a productive cough for at least 3 months in 2 consecutive years.

questions.text: The breath sounds that are discontinuous on auscultation in a patient with respiratory disease are:
questions.explanation: Crackles (A) are correct because they are short, explosive, discontinuous adventitious sounds produced by the sudden opening of collapsed small airways or by air moving through fluid, heard in pneumonia, pulmonary oedema, fibrosis and bronchiectasis (they are described as fine or coarse). Wheezes (B) are incorrect because they are continuous, high-pitched, musical sounds from narrowed airways (as in asthma and COPD). Stridor (C) is incorrect because it is a continuous, harsh, high-pitched sound heard on inspiration from upper airway obstruction. Shrills (D) is incorrect because it is not a recognised breath sound.

questions.text: A client with a subdural hematoma becomes restless and confused, with dilation of the pupils. The doctor orders Mannitol to:

options.C: Promote osmotic diuresis to decrease ICP
options.D: Draw water into the vascular system to increase BP

questions.explanation: Promote osmotic diuresis to decrease ICP (C) is correct because restlessness, confusion and pupil dilatation are signs of rising intracranial pressure, and mannitol is an osmotic diuretic that raises the osmolality of the blood, drawing water out of the brain tissue into the vessels, from where it is excreted by the kidneys, so that the intracranial pressure falls. The nurse monitors urine output (with a urinary catheter), serum osmolality and electrolytes, and neurological status. Reduce intraocular pressure (A) is incorrect because, although mannitol does lower intraocular pressure, that is not the reason it is given here. Prevent acute tubular necrosis (B) is incorrect because it is used for that purpose only in specific settings, and not in this case. Draw water into the vascular system to increase BP (D) is incorrect because the aim is to reduce brain swelling, and not to raise the blood pressure.

questions.text: Health messages for a patient with Myasthenia gravis on prevention of myasthenic and cholinergic crises include:

options.C: Doing all chores early in the day while less fatigued
options.D: Taking medications on time to maintain therapeutic blood levels

questions.explanation: Taking medications on time to maintain therapeutic blood levels (D) is correct because both crises are related to the dose and timing of the anticholinesterase drugs (such as pyridostigmine): too little or late a dose causes a myasthenic crisis (muscle weakness, respiratory failure), and too much causes a cholinergic crisis (excess acetylcholine, with abdominal cramps, diarrhoea, salivation, sweating and bradycardia and also weakness), so the drugs must be taken exactly on schedule, generally 30 to 45 minutes before meals. Eating large meals (A) is incorrect because chewing and swallowing are weak, so small frequent meals are advised. Muscle-strengthening exercises (B) is incorrect because exercise causes fatigue and weakness, so rest periods are advised. Doing all chores early in the day (C) is incorrect because, although energy conservation and planning activities for times of peak strength is good advice, it does not prevent the crises, and it is not the best answer.

questions.text: An early indicator of increased intracranial pressure is:
questions.explanation: Change in level of consciousness (C) is correct because the cerebral cortex and the reticular activating system are very sensitive to pressure and hypoxia, so restlessness, confusion, drowsiness or a falling Glasgow Coma Scale score is the earliest and most sensitive sign of rising intracranial pressure. Bradycardia (A) is incorrect because it is a late sign, part of Cushing's triad (bradycardia, hypertension with a widened pulse pressure, and irregular respirations). Decerebrate posturing (B) is incorrect because it is a late sign of brainstem damage. Unequal pupil size (D) is incorrect because it is a late sign caused by compression of the oculomotor nerve (an ipsilateral dilated, sluggish pupil).

questions.text: A correct statement about signs and symptoms of Gullain Barre Syndrome is that:

options.A: Unilateral and descending starting in the lower extremities
options.B: Symmetrical and ascending starting in the lower extremities
options.C: Symmetrical and ascending starting in the upper extremities
options.D: Symmetrical and descending starting in the upper extremities

questions.explanation: Symmetrical and ascending starting in the lower extremities (B) is correct because Guillain-Barre syndrome is an acute autoimmune demyelinating polyneuropathy, often after an infection (for example Campylobacter jejuni), in which weakness and tingling begin in the feet and legs, are bilateral and symmetrical, and ascend to the trunk, arms, face and respiratory muscles, with loss of deep tendon reflexes, so the vital capacity and the swallowing must be monitored closely (treatment is plasmapheresis or IV immunoglobulin, with ventilatory support when needed). Unilateral and descending (A), symmetrical and ascending from the upper extremities (C) and symmetrical and descending from the upper extremities (D) are incorrect because the paralysis is not unilateral, does not begin in the arms and is not descending (descending paralysis is typical of poliomyelitis and botulism).

questions.text: A life-threatening injury that is corrected by position is:
questions.explanation: Airway obstruction (D) is correct because the obstruction caused by the tongue falling back in an unconscious patient can be relieved at once by positioning: the head tilt and chin lift (or the jaw thrust if a cervical spine injury is suspected) or the recovery position, which opens the airway and drains secretions, and this is the first step in the airway part of the primary survey. Tension pneumothorax (A) is incorrect because it needs needle decompression and a chest drain. Flail chest (B) is incorrect because it needs oxygen, analgesia and, if severe, ventilatory support (positioning on the injured side is only a temporary measure). Open pneumothorax (C) is incorrect because it needs a three-sided occlusive dressing and a chest drain.

questions.text: Ms. A, 22 years old complained of lower abdominal pain, dizziness and feeling faint at triage. She should see the doctor within:
questions.explanation: Zero minutes (A) is correct because a young woman of reproductive age with lower abdominal pain, dizziness and near-fainting may have a ruptured ectopic pregnancy with internal bleeding and hypovolaemic shock, which is a life-threatening emergency, so she is triaged as red (emergency, priority 1) and needs immediate attention, with IV access, fluid resuscitation and urgent surgical review. In the triage categories, red patients are seen immediately (0 minutes), orange within about 10 to 15 minutes, yellow within about 30 to 60 minutes, and green can wait longer. 15 minutes (B), 30 minutes (C) and 60 minutes (D) are incorrect because they would delay care for a patient who may be bleeding and in shock.

questions.text: The theory exemplified by a 79-year-old retired actor who continues to pursue lifelong interests in swimming and singing is:
questions.explanation: Continuity (A) is correct because the continuity theory of ageing states that older adults adapt to ageing by maintaining the habits, interests, roles and relationships of earlier life, as the retired actor does by continuing swimming and singing. Developmental (B) is incorrect because developmental theories (for example Erikson's) describe the stages and tasks of life, with ego integrity versus despair in old age. Disengagement (C) is incorrect because this theory proposes that ageing involves a mutual, gradual withdrawal of the older person and society from each other, which is the opposite of what is described. Physical (D) is incorrect because it is a category of biological theories of ageing (such as wear and tear and free radical theory), and not a psychosocial theory. Activity theory, which holds that staying active gives successful ageing, is also close to this scenario, but continuity is the best fit for the lifelong interests.
